subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: A, B, C are three horses in a race. The probability of A to win the race is twice that of B, and the probability of B is twice that of C. What are the probabilities of A, B, C to win the race?

mark_split.label: Events; write P(A), P(B) in terms of P(C)
The three are disjoint and exhaustive, so the sum is 1

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the three winning probabilities — how A and B are written in terms of C, why the three add to 1, and the values.
insider_note: Two facts are needed and both must be written: only one horse wins (disjoint), and one of the three does win (exhaustive). Together they make the three probabilities add to 1.

steps.label: Write P(A), P(B) in terms of P(C)
steps.margin_note: First mark. P(A) = 2P(B) and P(B) = 2P(C), so P(A) = 4P(C). Everything is now in one unknown.

steps.why: Two relations and three unknowns need one more equation; writing all three in terms of P(C) leaves exactly one unknown for that equation.

steps.label: Disjoint and exhaustive: sum = 1
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Only one horse wins (disjoint) and one of them does win (A ∪ B ∪ C = S), so P(A) + P(B) + P(C) = P(S) = 1.

lines.text: Only one horse can win, so A, B, C are disjoint;
one of them wins, so A ∪ B ∪ C = S.

recall.must_convey: That A, B, C are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so P(A) + P(B) + P(C) = 1.

steps.why: Disjoint makes the union probability a plain sum; exhaustive makes that union the whole sample space, probability 1. Both are needed for the equation.
common_mistakes: Writing the sum = 1 with no reason.
Saying only "mutually exclusive" — that gives ≤ 1, not = 1.
